leichttraben-komplett: frage
Why do riders keep standing up and sitting down in trot?
warum
That's called rising trot. It takes the weight off your horse's back – and makes the trot much more comfortable for you.
zweitakt
The trot is a two-beat gait: two legs always land at the same time, diagonally opposite each other.
wie
In rising trot, you move forwards and upwards from your hips on one beat – and sit softly back down on the next.
aufab
Up, down, up, down – in your horse's rhythm.
haende
Your hands stay still in the same place. Your knees stay springy, and your heels stay down.
treiben
And when do you use your legs? Always as you sit! Give a short squeeze with both calves – when you rise, your legs stay relaxed.
warumtreiben
Because when you sit, the inside hind leg is just pushing off. That's exactly when your leg helps.
fuss
Now all that's missing is the correct diagonal.
schulter
You rise when your horse's outside shoulder moves forward.
falsch
On the wrong diagonal? No problem: just sit for one extra beat – and you're back on the right one.
wechsel
Every time you change the rein, you change your diagonal too.
merke
Remember: outside shoulder forward – you're up. And use your legs as you sit.
leichter-sitz: Why do riders sometimes half stand up in canter?
That's the light seat. Your weight comes out of the saddle – so your horse can move its back freely.
You use it, for example, to warm up, out hacking or when jumping.
One: lift your bottom a tiny bit. Your weight goes down into the stirrups.
Two: lean your upper body slightly forward.
Three: heels down. Your knees act like springs.
Four: your hands follow your horse's neck.
Really important: don't hold on to the reins. Your balance comes from your legs.
Remember: bottom up, heels down, hands follow.
pferd-lenken: How do you actually steer a horse?
Not just with the reins! You steer with your whole body.
One: look where you want to go.
Two: shift your weight a tiny bit to the inside.
Three: your inside leg works on the girth, your outside leg lies slightly behind it.
Four: the inside rein shows the way, the outside rein gives – but keeps the contact.
Never pull on just one rein! Your horse will turn its head, but not its body.
Remember: first look, then sit, then leg and hand.
innen-aussen: Inside leg, outside rein – what do inside and outside actually mean?
The inside is the side your horse is bent towards. On a circle, that's the side towards the middle.
Your inside leg works on the girth. Your horse bends around it.
Your outside leg lies slightly behind and makes sure the hindquarters don't swing out.
The outside rein controls the shoulder. The inside rein only asks for a little flexion – you can just see the inside eye.
If you only pull on the inside, the neck bends – but the shoulder drifts out.
The answer is framing: your horse moves between your aids – like between two rails.
Remember: inside drives, outside holds – so the shoulder stays where it belongs.
anreiten-durchparieren: frage
How do you tell your horse: let's go – or: time to slow down?
hilfen
You have three aids for this: your weight, your legs and your reins. They always work together.
hp
Before every change of gait comes a half-halt. It means: attention, something's about to happen!
hpwie
Here's how it works: you sit deep for a moment and tighten your tummy muscles. Your legs stay on. And your hand closes briefly – and then softens again straight away.
hpzieh
Important: the hand doesn't pull. It just holds for a moment and then softens again.
schritt
From halt to walk: first a half-halt. Then both legs ask on the girth. Your pelvis moves forward with the horse, and your hand gives a little – so your horse can move off.
schritt2
As soon as it walks, your legs lie quietly against its sides again.
trab
From walk to trot: again, a half-halt. Then both legs ask a little more clearly, and your hand allows your horse forward.
trab2
Sit the first few strides. After that, you can go into rising trot.
galopp
From trot to canter: sit to the trot and give a half-halt – ideally in a corner or on a circle.
galopp2
Your weight goes a little more to the inside. Your inside leg asks on the girth. Your outside leg lies a hand's width behind it.
galopp3
The inside rein asks for a little flexion to the inside, the outside rein holds – and as your horse strikes off, your hand gives.
galopp4
And off it goes into canter – with the outside hind leg first.
runter
To slow down, you give several half-halts in a row. That's called a downward transition.
gt
From canter to trot: sit deep, keep your legs on, close and soften your hand – until your horse trots. Then your hand becomes light again straight away.
ts
From trot to walk: sit to the trot and give a few more half-halts until your horse walks.
warum
And why do your legs stay on when you slow down? So your horse keeps stepping under its belly with its hind legs and doesn't just fall onto its forehand.
gp
From walk to halt: that's the full halt. Several half-halts in quick succession, until your horse stands still.
gp2
Once it's standing quietly on all four legs, your hand becomes light. And you praise your horse.
treppe
At first, you go down from canter to halt step by step: canter, trot, walk, halt. On every step of the staircase, you give half-halts.
profi
Experienced riders and well-schooled horses can later make bigger jumps – for example straight from canter to walk.
merke
Remember: a half-halt means attention. A full halt means stop. Your legs take you forward – and after every aid, your hand becomes light again.
